topic: the concept of a simple pendulum's period formula

easy.text: What does the 'period' of a pendulum refer to?

options.text: The time for one complete back-and-forth swing
options.feedback: Correct -- period is the total time for the pendulum to return to its starting position after one full swing cycle.

options.text: The highest point the pendulum reaches
options.feedback: That describes the amplitude or maximum displacement, not the period (a measure of time).

options.text: The weight of the pendulum's bob
options.feedback: Weight is a separate physical property, unrelated to the definition of a pendulum's period.

options.text: The material the pendulum is made of
options.feedback: Material composition isn't related to the definition of period, which is specifically a measure of time.

medium.text: If you increase the length of a pendulum's string, what generally happens to its period?

options.text: The period increases (the pendulum swings more slowly)
options.feedback: Correct -- a longer pendulum takes more time to complete each swing, resulting in a longer period.

options.text: The period decreases (the pendulum swings faster)
options.feedback: This is backwards -- increasing the length actually makes each swing take LONGER, increasing the period, not decreasing it.

options.text: The period stays exactly the same, regardless of length
options.feedback: Length is actually one of the primary factors affecting a pendulum's period -- changing it does change the period.
Changing the length doesn't stop the pendulum -- it continues swinging, just at a different (in this case slower) rate.

hard.text: The period of a simple pendulum is proportional to the SQUARE ROOT of its length (T ∝ √L). If you want to double a pendulum's period, by what factor must you increase its length?

options.feedback: Correct -- since period depends on the square root of length, doubling the period requires quadrupling the length (√4=2).
This would only double the period if period were directly proportional to length, but it's actually proportional to the SQUARE ROOT of length, requiring a larger length increase.
This overstates the needed increase -- quadrupling (not increasing by 8x) the length is what doubles the period, based on the square root relationship.

options.text: The length has no effect on achieving a longer period
options.feedback: Length absolutely does affect the period -- increasing it appropriately (quadrupling, in this case) is exactly how you'd double the period.

easy.hard: This measures the duration of a single, complete repeating oscillation cycle.
easy.medium: This is how long it takes for the pendulum to swing there and back once.
easy.easy: This is how long it takes the pendulum to swing there and back once.

medium.hard: A longer physical length generally corresponds to a proportionally longer time needed to complete each full swing cycle.
medium.medium: A longer pendulum takes more time to complete each full swing.
medium.easy: A longer pendulum takes longer to swing back and forth.

hard.hard: Since period scales with the square root of length, achieving a given multiplicative change in period requires squaring that same multiplicative factor for length.
hard.medium: Since period depends on the square root of length, you need to square the desired period-doubling factor to find the needed length factor.
hard.easy: Since doubling the period needs the SQUARE ROOT of the length to double, the length itself needs to go up by 4 times (since √4=2).
